source: MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension (នាយកដ្ឋានផ្សព្វផ្សាយកសិកម្ម), "បច្ចេកទេសដាំដុះសណ្តែកបាយ" (Mung Bean Cultivation Techniques handbook), Kingdom of Cambodia, MAFF, published by the Department of Agricultural Extension. Reference list on the closing page cites additional 2003-dated MAFF/agricultural-extension source booklets on mung bean varieties, seed production, and pest management, plus several international references (Plant Resources of South-East Asia Vol. I, 1992; Talekar & Skinner, Field Guide to Insect Pests of Tropical Asia, 1995; Nelson, Insect Pests of Vegetables, Philippines, 1969; Mung Bean Adaptation Trial, Kbalkoh Station 1996-2000, CLV Network; and a 1991 Bangkok workshop proceedings on Yellow Mosaic Virus). No elibrary.maff.gov.kh URL is visible on the scanned pages provided, so none is given here. Uploaded as a 38-page scanned PDF; no embedded text layer, all content read visually from page images. This is Source C for crop/mung_bean in this knowledge base (Sources A-B were processed in Batch 42).
text: The source describes two harvest approaches. (1) Harvest for seed stock: harvest only fully mature pods, identified by pod color changing from green to a darker/dry tone before pods shatter and drop seed on their own; because maturity varies across a field, harvesting should be staged (checking repeatedly) rather than done all at once, and timing should avoid both premature and overly late harvest. After harvest, pods are sun-dried for roughly 2-3 days before threshing; only seed meeting a uniform-seed-shape standard is retained for the next planting. (2) Harvest for commercial/consumption product: once the crop reaches roughly 100 days, pods are harvested progressively as they mature, sun-dried 2-3 days, then threshed, with the source specifying drying to roughly 13-14% grain moisture before storage. Harvest timing depends on variety maturity group: early varieties at roughly 60-65 days, medium varieties at roughly 65-70 days, and late varieties at roughly 70-75 days after planting; because pods do not all mature simultaneously, 2-3 sequential harvest rounds are typical, timed to variety and pod maturity pattern. Yield potential by type: black gram (សណ្តែកប្រេង) yield is given as roughly 560-1,500 kg/ha, averaging roughly 800-1,050 kg/ha in Cambodia; the mung bean/green-gram type yield is given as roughly 500-1,800 kg/ha, averaging roughly 700-1,000 kg/ha in Cambodia.
